## Executive Summary

Most people unlock an account without giving it a thought: type a password look at a phone tap a code and that is it. For a person who's visually impaired almost every step in that process can quietly fail. A QR code that cannot be seen a CAPTCHA that assumes the user can see and read or an error message that changes color but has no clear text. This proposal outlines a web-based authentication system our team is creating for the Computer Security module. It treats accessibility not as something added at the end. As a rule that influences the security design from the very first choice.

The system uses email and password login combined with an authentication factor based on TOTP. It also includes a recovery code as a backup when the authenticator app is not available. It has rate-limiting and lockout features to stop force and enumeration attacks. All of this is wrapped in a frontend that works completely with a keyboard and a screen reader. In this design TOTP is the step of authentication. An app like Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator is the tool used to create the six-digit TOTP code. MFA enrollment gives both a QR code and the TOTP secret as text making QR scanning optional of required.

The system is built so that a person who is visually impaired can go through the authentication process on their own. This includes logging in with a password enrolling for TOTP using the secret when needed verifying TOTP getting feedback and using a recovery code. Every choice made in the design is supported by a known standard (NIST SP 800-63B the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, RFC 6238 or WCAG 2.1). Every assumption we made to keep the project for a team of five, over one semester is clearly stated instead of being left unspoken.

## 1. Introduction and Motivation

According to the World Health Organization, at least 2.2 billion people around the world have some form of vision impairment [1]. For many of them, everyday digital tasks like logging into an account can be difficult, especially when the steps depend on being able to see the screen clearly. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is widely used to protect accounts and sensitive data. It adds extra security, but many MFA methods still assume that every user can see and follow visual instructions. This can include scanning a QR code during setup, recognising a green tick or a red cross, or completing a visual CAPTCHA. For users with visual impairments, these steps can make it hard to log in or even set up MFA on their own.

Our motivation for this project comes from this problem. Security and accessibility are often treated as two separate things, but we wanted to consider both together from the beginning. As a small team, we wanted to explore how an MFA system could protect an account while also being easier for visually impaired users to use independently. A QR code or a colour-coded error may seem like a small detail, but it can become a real barrier when a user cannot see it. So our main question is, how can we remove these barriers without making the security weaker? Finding a balance between these two needs is what guides the design choices in this proposal.

## 2. Problem Statement

Traditional MFA systems often rely on visual steps or instructions. These include image-based CAPTCHAs, QR codes with no text alternative during setup, and status messages that only use colour. For someone with a visual impairment who uses a screen reader or screen magnifier, these features can make a normal sign-in process difficult or sometimes impossible. For example, asking a user to scan a QR code without giving another option can stop them from setting up MFA independently, even if they can use the time-based one-time password (TOTP) method itself.

At the same time, making a system accessible should not mean reducing its security. If a system is easy to use but also easy to break into, we are just replacing one problem with another. So this project focuses on two things: building a secure MFA system, and making sure visually impaired users can set it up and sign in without depending on sight. Both needs have to be considered together, while keeping proper protection against brute-force attempts, replay attacks and code guessing.

## 3. Project Objectives

- Build a working email and password login system, using the password as the first

authentication factor and Argon2id to securely hash stored passwords.

- Add TOTP as the second authentication factor, with support for common

authenticator apps. The app is just the tool that generates the code, not an extra factor by itself. During MFA setup, users will have an accessible manual entry option, along with an optional QR code.

- Provide one-time recovery codes so users can still access their account if they lose

access to their authenticator app.

- Protect the login system against brute-force attempts and account enumeration. This

will include rate limiting, temporary lockouts, generic error messages and audit logging, without relying on visual-only checks like image CAPTCHAs.

- Build the frontend to meet WCAG 2.1 accessibility requirements, making sure every

authentication screen works with a keyboard and that screen readers announce the instructions, errors and status messages properly.

- Make sure users can complete the whole authentication process independently. This

includes setting up MFA, entering TOTP codes, understanding errors and using recovery codes, without needing help from another person.

- Document and explain the reasons behind each design choice and assumption,

referring to recognised standards and guidance such as NIST, OWASP, RFC 6238 and WCAG, as required by the module.

## 4. Scope

This project focuses on secure login, multi-factor authentication, account recovery and accessibility. It is not intended to be a full enterprise identity and access management platform, as stated in A45.

The system uses email and password for login, with the password acting as the first authentication factor and TOTP as the second. Users can generate their TOTP codes through an authenticator app, such as Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator. The app itself is only a tool for generating the code, so it does not count as another authentication factor.

During MFA enrolment, users will have an optional QR code and an accessible text version of the TOTP setup secret for manual entry. This gives visually impaired users another way to complete setup if scanning the QR code is difficult or not possible.

The web application will support keyboard navigation, screen readers, clear status and error messages, and proper focus management. Users should be able to complete password login, MFA enrolment, TOTP verification and recovery-code use on their own, without needing assistance.

The project does not include building or replacing an authenticator app. We assume that the chosen app works with the accessibility features available on the user's phone. Email verification, SMS OTP, social login and CAPTCHA are outside the scope. These are left out to keep the project manageable and avoid extra dependencies, while visual CAPTCHAs would also create accessibility barriers.

All assumptions that define the scope are listed in Appendix A. Each team member also explains the assumptions relevant to their work in their Individual Design Document.

### 4.1 Functional Requirements

These requirements explain what the system needs to do and the features it will provide.

| ID | Requirement | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FR1 | Password authentication | Registered users must be able to log in with their email and password. The backend will check the password against the stored hash. |
| FR2 | Two-step authentication | For accounts with MFA enabled, users must pass both password and TOTP verification before getting full access. Completing only the password step must not allow access to protected resources. |
| FR3 | Accessible MFA enrolment | MFA setup must include an optional QR code and a readable setup secret that users can copy. This allows users to set up a compatible authenticator app without scanning the QR code. |
| FR4 | Enrolment confirmation | The system must check a code generated by the user's configured authenticator app before enabling MFA on the account. |
| FR5 | TOTP verification | The system must verify six-digit TOTP codes using a 30-second time step. Invalid codes, codes outside the accepted time window and codes already accepted for that time step must be rejected. |
| FR6 | Recovery-code generation | When MFA is enabled, the system must generate ten cryptographically secure, one-time recovery codes. These must be presented in an accessible format so the user can save them. |
| FR7 | Account recovery | Recovery codes must be checked against their stored hashes. A valid code can be used once to start recovery. The user must then choose a new password and set up MFA again. |
| FR8 | Session management | The system must manage authentication through server-side sessions referenced by secure HttpOnly cookies. It must support logout and session revocation, and reject protected requests made with invalid or revoked sessions. |
| FR9 | Rate limiting and temporary lockout | Redis must be used to limit repeated login, TOTP verification and recovery attempts. Repeated failures must trigger a temporary lockout based on the configured policy. |
| FR10 | Accessible feedback | Users must receive clear instructions and text-based success and error messages. Dynamic messages must be announced by screen readers, with focus moved to a suitable place when screens change or errors occur. |
| FR11 | Generic authentication errors | Login and recovery failure messages must not reveal whether an account exists. |
| FR12 | Audit logging | Successful and failed authentication and recovery attempts must be recorded in a PostgreSQL audit log. Passwords, TOTP codes and recovery codes must never be included. |

### 4.2 Non-Functional Requirements

These requirements describe how the system should behave in terms of accessibility, security, reliability and ease of maintenance.

| ID | Requirement | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NFR1 | Accessibility | Every authentication screen must meet the applicable WCAG 2.1 requirements. All controls must work with a keyboard and have a logical focus order, visible focus indicators, clear labels and screen-reader support. Instructions and feedback must not rely only on colour, icons or images. |
| NFR2 | Independent usability | Users must be able to complete login, MFA setup, TOTP verification and account recovery without sighted assistance, using a compatible accessible authenticator app. Instructions must be easy to understand and explain how to correct input errors. |
| NFR3 | Credential confidentiality | Passwords must be stored as Argon2id hashes, and recovery codes must only be stored as hashes. TOTP setup secrets and session identifiers must be protected from unauthorised access and kept out of logs. |
| NFR4 | Secure communication | The frontend and backend must communicate over HTTPS in production. Session cookies must use the Secure and HttpOnly attributes. |
| NFR5 | Data integrity | Authentication and recovery operations must keep account data consistent. Even when requests arrive at the same time, the system must prevent a recovery code or an already accepted TOTP code for the same time step from being reused successfully. |
| NFR6 | Reliable failure handling | Invalid input, expired authentication state and service failures must produce controlled, accessible responses. These failures must not bypass authentication or reveal internal error details. |
| NFR7 | Compatibility | The system must work with compatible TOTP authenticator apps. Testing must cover browser and screen-reader combinations using NVDA or VoiceOver, with the tested combinations and any limitations documented. |
| NFR8 | Maintainability and testability | The backend must remain one application with separate modules for authentication, MFA, recovery and security controls. API behaviour must be documented through OpenAPI, and the modules must support automated unit and integration tests. |
| NFR9 | Reproducible deployment | The application and its required services must run through Docker Compose for local development and demonstration. Setup steps, configuration requirements and database migrations must be documented. |

## 5. Proposed System Overview

The system uses a single-page React application connected to a FastAPI backend over HTTPS. PostgreSQL stores the application data, while Redis keeps track of failed login attempts, MFA attempts and account recovery requests.

We chose to use one structured backend instead of splitting the system into several microservices. With five members and one semester to complete the project, we felt this would be easier to manage. Having one backend codebase that everyone understands also makes it easier to review the security controls and keep things consistent.

The authentication process has two steps. First, users enter their email and password. They then complete the second step by entering a TOTP code generated by an authenticator app on their phone. The app is the tool used to generate this code, so it does not count as an additional factor on top of TOTP.

During MFA setup, users can either scan a QR code or copy the TOTP setup secret and enter it manually into their authenticator app. The manual option is especially useful for visually impaired users who may find scanning a QR code difficult. This way, setting up MFA does not depend only on being able to see the screen.

The frontend will support keyboard navigation and work with screen readers throughout the whole process. This includes logging in, setting up MFA, entering a TOTP code, understanding error messages and recovering an account. We want users to complete all these steps independently, with clear instructions at each stage.

Figure 1 shows how these components connect and work together.

![Diagram from page 9](data:image/png;base64,)

### 5.1 Core Authentication

Users first log in with their email and password, with the password acting as the first authentication factor. Passwords are hashed using Argon2id, following the guidance in the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet [2]. They are not encrypted or stored in a form that can be recovered later.

We chose server-side sessions, referenced by a secure HttpOnly cookie, instead of JWTs. The main reason is that we can revoke a session immediately when needed. This is useful when handling account lockouts and recovery, where an existing session may need to be stopped.

The login form uses semantic HTML controls, clear labels and keyboard-accessible navigation. This allows users to complete the first step with a screen reader or keyboard, without depending on sight. If login fails, the interface explains the problem through text rather than just showing a different colour. The backend is responsible for checking whether the session is valid and the user is authenticated.

![Diagram from page 10](data:image/png;base64,)

### 5.2 Multi-Factor Authentication (TOTP)

The second authentication factor uses a Time-Based One-Time Password, or TOTP, following RFC 6238. Users generate the code through a compatible authenticator app, such as Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator. The app itself does not count as an extra authentication factor. It generates the six-digit code that the backend checks as proof that the user has access to the enrolled TOTP secret.

We chose TOTP over SMS codes because it does not need a phone network or an SMS provider to generate codes. This avoids problems like delayed messages or failed delivery.

Once set up, a compatible authenticator app can generate the codes even without an internet connection.

During MFA enrolment, the system provides an optional QR code and a text version of the TOTP setup secret. Users who cannot see or scan the QR code can copy or type this secret into their authenticator app instead. This gives visually impaired users a way to complete setup without depending on the QR code.

After enrolment, the authenticator app generates a six-digit code every 30 seconds. The user enters this code on the web application's MFA page. After the password step, the backend checks the submitted code and only grants a fully authenticated session if verification succeeds.

The MFA page will provide clear instructions, proper labels, focus management, and accessible success and error messages. We are not building the authenticator app as part of this project. So the complete process also depends on the chosen app working with the accessibility features on the user's device.

![Diagram from page 11](data:image/png;base64,)

### 5.3 Account Recovery

Users may lose access to their authenticator app, so we need a way for them to recover their account. When MFA is turned on, the system generates ten one-time recovery codes using Python's secrets module. We only store a hash of each code, similar to how passwords are protected. Each recovery code can be used just once to begin the recovery process.

The recovery screens will support keyboard navigation and screen readers. This allows visually impaired users to follow the steps on their own, without needing someone else to read the screen. After using a recovery code successfully, the user needs to set up MFA again and choose a new password. We added this step because they may have lost control of their device or login details.

![Diagram from page 12](data:image/png;base64,)

### 5.4 Security Hardening

All authentication endpoints, including login, MFA verification and account recovery, will use Redis-based rate limiting. Temporary lockouts will also apply after repeated failed attempts. Successful and failed authentication attempts will be recorded in a PostgreSQL audit log. It records what happened, but never includes passwords, TOTP codes or recovery codes.

We thought about adding a CAPTCHA because it is common in login systems. But visual CAPTCHAs can make the process difficult for users who depend on screen readers or keyboard navigation. So we chose rate limiting and temporary lockouts to help limit repeated attacks. The audit logs also help us track suspicious activity. This way, users can go through the security checks without having to solve a visual puzzle.

### 5.5 Accessibility and Frontend Design

The frontend uses semantic HTML elements such as `<button>`, `<label>` and `<input>`, styled with Tailwind CSS. Using these standard elements gives us built-in keyboard and screen-reader support, without having to recreate these behaviours through custom widgets.

When the screen changes, focus will move to a suitable place so users can understand where they are and continue with the next step. Form errors will appear as text and be announced through an ARIA live region, rather than relying only on colour. The frontend will check the backend session to confirm whether the user is logged in. Once a session is revoked, the backend will reject further authenticated requests, and the interface will update when it receives that response.

Users will not need to scan a QR code to set up MFA. During TOTP enrolment, the setup secret will also be available as text that screen readers can read. Users can copy or manually enter it into a compatible authenticator app. The QR code will still be there as an optional method.

The TOTP verification screen will have a clearly labelled input field and accessible instructions. Success and error messages will be shown in text and announced to screen-reader users. We will avoid using colour or icons as the only way to explain what happened.

Accessibility will be considered throughout the authentication process, including login, MFA enrolment, TOTP verification, recovery-code entry and error handling. We are not building our own authenticator app, so we assume the chosen app supports the user's accessibility needs. We will check this assumption during end-to-end testing.

## 6.0 Technology Stack

The stack below was chosen to keep the team working with familiar, well-documented tools, so that effort goes into the security and accessibility design rather than fighting unfamiliar infrastructure.

| Layer | Technology | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frontend | React + Vite | Fast to build, clean component structure |
| UI | Tailwind CSS | Quick to build clean, accessible interfaces on top of native HTML elements |
| Database | PostgreSQL | Reliable, well-understood storage for account and audit data |
| Backend | Python FastAPI | Fast API development with built-in validation and OpenAPI docs |
| ORM / migrations | SQLAlchemy + Alembic | Standard, well-supported PostgreSQL integration for FastAPI |
| Password hashing | Argon2id | Current OWASP-recommended password-hashing algorithm |
| Session handling | Server-side sessions + secure,cookies | Simpler and more easily revocable than JWT for this project |
| MFA | TOTP via pyotp | Interoperable with Google Authenticator,Microsoft Authenticator, etc |
| Recovery codes | Python secrets + hashed storage | Cryptographically secure, single-use recovery mechanism |
| Rate limiting | Redis | Fast, TTL-native store for login/MFA attempt counters |
| Security logging | PostgreSQL | Simple and sufficient at this project's scale; no ELK stack needed |
| Deployment | Docker Compose | Reproducible local development and demo environment |

## 7. Team Structure and Responsibilities

We divided the system into five main areas, with each member taking responsibility for designing and implementing one part. This makes it easier for everyone to manage their work and test their own module before bringing the parts together into one complete authentication system.

Member 1 is responsible for the system architecture and core authentication, including login and session handling. This forms the base for the other members' work, since MFA, account recovery, security controls and the frontend all need to work with the same login and session structure. So we need to agree on this part early to help everyone develop their modules consistently.

## 8. Testing and Evaluation Strategy

We will test the system from different angles, because getting the features to work does not always mean they are secure or accessible. Our testing will cover individual modules, the complete authentication process, security controls and accessibility.

- Unit and integration testing: We will test password hashing, TOTP secret

generation and verification, recovery-code use, rate-limit counting and session handling. These tests will use a separate test database and Redis instance.

- End-to-end testing: We will check the full journey from login through MFA to the

dashboard. This will also include completing the process using only a keyboard, with no mouse interaction.

- MFA accessibility testing: We will check whether users can enrol in MFA using the

manual setup secret without looking at the QR code. We will also test entering a six-digit TOTP code, receiving accessible success and error messages, and completing the recovery-code flow.

- Security testing: We will test resistance to brute-force attempts and check that

previously accepted TOTP codes and used recovery codes cannot be reused. We will also compare response messages to check whether they reveal if an account exists.

- Accessibility testing: We will use automated tools such as axe-core, along with

manual screen-reader testing using NVDA or VoiceOver. These checks will cover every authentication screen.

- Independent completion: We will check whether the whole authentication journey

can be completed without another person's help. The chosen authenticator app is an external dependency, so we will also test how it works with the mobile device's accessibility features and document whether our accessibility assumption holds.

## 9. Expected Outcomes

By the end of the project, we expect to have a working authentication system that can be deployed using Docker. Our aim is for a visually impaired user to complete the whole process independently, without needing someone else to read the screen or guide them.

The system will support:

- Email and password login, with passwords securely hashed using Argon2id.
- TOTP as the second authentication factor.
- MFA enrolment through an optional QR code or a readable setup secret that users

can enter manually.

- Six-digit TOTP codes generated through a compatible authenticator app.

- TOTP verification using web controls that work with keyboards and screen readers.

- Single-use recovery codes for users who lose access to their authenticator app.

- Rate limiting and temporary lockouts to restrict repeated attempts, generic responses

to reduce account enumeration, and audit logs to monitor activity, without relying on visual CAPTCHAs.

We also want to understand where security and accessibility cause difficulties for each other in practice. Our testing should help us explain which design choices create barriers and which alternatives work well for both needs. For example, we will evaluate whether rate limiting and temporary lockouts give suitable protection against repeated attempts while keeping the process accessible without visual CAPTCHAs. These findings will give us an evidence-based answer to the question that started the project.

## 10. Conclusion

Security and accessibility are often handled separately, by different people or at different stages of a project. In this proposal, we consider both from the beginning. We make our assumptions clear and use recognised standards to explain the design choices, instead of choosing something only because it is easy to build.

The system uses email and password login, with the password as the first authentication factor and TOTP as the second. An authenticator app generates the TOTP code, but the app itself does not count as another factor. During MFA enrolment, users can choose between scanning a QR code and manually entering the TOTP setup secret. This means they do not have to depend on sight to complete setup.

The web interface will support keyboards and screen readers throughout the authentication process. Recovery codes will also give users a way to recover their account if they lose access to the authenticator app.

We divided the work into five areas so each member has a clear part to design, build and test. The shared architecture described in Section 5 keeps these parts connected as one system. Through this project, we aim to show how secure authentication, account recovery and accessibility can work together within what our team can realistically complete in one semester.

| A32 | API documentation | FastAPI OpenAPI/Swagger |
